opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing to recognize is that the uncertainty itself is the central fact we have to plan around. People often argue about whether transformative AI is five years away or thirty, as though we have to settle that before we can act. But institutions don't get to wait for that resolution. So the question becomes: what commitments make sense across that whole range of possibilities?

One way I think about it is as a portfolio problem. If timelines are short, the things that matter most are fairly immediate: the ability to evaluate frontier systems, some visibility into what the leading labs are doing, and emergency capacities, so that a government could actually act quickly if a dangerous capability showed up. If timelines are long, what matters more is building durable institutions, international agreements, and expertise inside government. The good news is that many of these overlap. Building state capacity to understand AI is valuable in nearly every scenario. So you want to prioritize the robust actions first, the ones you wouldn't regret whichever world we're in.

The second point is about the asymmetry of errors. If we prepare for short timelines and they turn out to be long, we've spent some money and political capital a bit early, and we may have imposed some regulatory friction. That's a real cost, and I don't want to dismiss it. But if we assume long timelines and they turn out to be short, we could find ourselves facing an enormously consequential technology with no institutions able to respond. Those mistakes aren't symmetric, and that should push us toward taking the earlier scenarios seriously even if they aren't our median expectation.

There's a caveat, though. Political credibility is a finite resource. If advocates keep saying "this is coming in two years" and it doesn't, you burn trust and make it harder to act when it actually matters. So I think we should be honest about the uncertainty rather than overstating confidence in any particular date. The case for action doesn't depend on being sure it's soon. It rests on a meaningful chance that it's soon, combined with very high stakes.

Finally, I'd favour commitments that are conditional or adaptive. Rather than fixing a policy to a calendar date, you tie obligations to observable triggers: when systems reach certain capability thresholds, additional requirements kick in. That approach has been gaining traction, and I think it's wise, because it lets people who disagree about timelines agree on the policy. The sceptic can say, "Fine, I don't think we'll hit that threshold for decades, so this costs me little," and the person worried about short timelines gets protection if they're right. Designing institutions so they respond to evidence as it arrives, rather than to our current guesses, is probably the most important lesson uncertainty teaches us.

r001.rationale: The response says to take short timelines seriously because an early arrival could leave governments without institutions able to respond, and recommends robust preparation across timeline scenarios.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss compromising principles to appeal to powerful AI developers or governance actors.

r003.rationale: It does not mention America’s future alignment with allies or an American national AI programme.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a European AI alternative or compare its feasibility on two-year and ten-year timelines.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that uncertainty about timelines is not an argument for doing nothing. It's quite common to hear people say, "Well, we don't know whether transformative AI is five years away or fifty, so it's premature to commit to anything." But that gets the logic backwards. If you genuinely don't know, that's precisely the situation where you want institutions that are robust across a range of outcomes, rather than ones that only make sense if a particular forecast comes true.

The way I'd frame it is that we should be designing commitments that are cheap if timelines turn out to be long and extremely valuable if they turn out to be short. Things like building the capacity to measure and evaluate frontier systems, establishing clear lines of reporting between labs and governments, creating international forums where the major players actually talk to each other, agreeing on what kinds of evidence would trigger stronger action. None of those are wasted if AI progress slows down. They're the kind of institutional infrastructure you'd want anyway, and they can sit there at relatively low cost. But if progress is fast, having them already in place could be the difference between a managed transition and a chaotic one.

Where I'd be more cautious is with commitments that are brittle to the timeline being wrong in either direction. If you lock in something highly restrictive on the assumption that dangerous capabilities are imminent, and then they don't materialise for twenty years, you risk a backlash that discredits the whole project of taking this seriously, and you may lose the ability to act when it actually matters. Equally, if you build everything around a slow scenario and the fast one happens, you've essentially bet the world on being right.

So I think the honest answer is that uncertainty pushes you toward adaptive institutions rather than fixed policies. You want mechanisms that can ratchet up as evidence accumulates, with pre-agreed thresholds so that the ratcheting isn't a political fight every time. And you want to resist the temptation to treat the median forecast as if it were the plan. The tails matter enormously here, because the downside of being unprepared for a short timeline is so much worse than the cost of being slightly over-prepared for a long one. That asymmetry, more than any particular estimate of when things will happen, is what I think should be driving the institutional design.

r001.rationale: The response urges building institutional capacity in advance because fast AI progress could arrive before institutions are prepared, making preparation valuable despite timeline uncertainty.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss compromising principles to appeal to powerful AI actors.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention America’s future alignment with allies or an American national AI programme.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss a European AI alternative or compare two-year and ten-year timelines.

astra-6.text:
I think uncertainty should make us wary of tying policy to a single date. We don’t know whether the most consequential developments are a few years away or several decades away, and we need institutions that can function across that range.

That means distinguishing between commitments to principles and commitments to particular mechanisms. We can make a durable commitment that powerful AI systems should face serious scrutiny before they’re deployed, while allowing the methods of scrutiny to change as we learn more. You want the commitment to safety to be stable, and the technical details to be revisable.

There’s also a danger that uncertainty becomes an excuse for delay. If timelines might be short, then building expertise, developing evaluation methods, and establishing channels for international cooperation are urgent, because those things take time. And if timelines turn out to be longer, that work can still be valuable.

So I’d favour starting now on measures that make sense across a wide range of futures, with explicit opportunities to review them. The aim is to avoid both complacency and locking ourselves into arrangements that depend on a forecast we shouldn’t be very confident in.

r001.rationale: It urges preparation for potentially short timelines, but does not say early transformative AI could arrive when institutions are least prepared.

r002.rationale: It supports stable safety principles, but does not warn against compromising them to appeal to powerful AI actors.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss America’s future alignment with allies or commitments to a national AI programme.

r004.rationale: It does not discuss a European AI alternative or compare two-year and ten-year timelines.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the uncertainty should make us wary of tying our whole strategy to a particular date. If you build your policy around the assumption that transformative AI is coming in five years, you can make mistakes if it takes fifty. But assuming we have fifty years is itself a very consequential bet.

So I’d distinguish between commitments to particular policies and commitments to having the capacity to respond. You might want to revise a particular regulatory requirement as the evidence changes. But building technical expertise within government, developing ways to assess dangerous capabilities, and establishing channels for international cooperation are valuable across quite a wide range of timelines. Those things also take time, so uncertainty isn’t a good reason to postpone them.

The aim would be durable institutions with adaptable policies. And ideally you’d agree in advance on what kinds of evidence would justify stronger action. Otherwise, there’s a danger that every new development simply produces another argument about whether we should wait.

We don’t need certainty about when the risks will arrive to make a serious commitment to managing them.

r001.rationale: The candidate favors building response capacity across timelines, but does not specifically recommend hedging against early transformative AI because institutions could be least prepared then.
